select
    [address_id],
    [customer_id],
    [city]
from (
    select
        cast([address_id] as int) as [address_id],
        cast([customer_id] as int) as [customer_id],
        cast([city] as varchar(8000)) as [city],
        row_number() over (partition by [address_id] order by (select null)) as [_krusgraph_row]
    from {{ source('shop', 'addresses') }} as s

-- fct_order_items: one row per order_items row (order_id+line_no).
-- Generated by Krusgraph for dbt-fabric 1.12 (Fabric Data Warehouse T-SQL). A draft: review it. Nothing was created or run.
-- Joined only over relationships whose target key was counted unique (many-to-one), each over its safest path:
--   order_items.order_id -> orders.order_id (R1): holds for all 134 rows with a value
--   order_items.product_id -> products.product_id (R1): holds for all 134 rows with a value
--   products.category_id -> categories.id (R1): holds for all 8 rows with a value
--   orders.customer_id -> customers.customer_id (R1): holds for all 60 rows with a value
-- Left out: products.list_price: an amount on products; this mart has one row per order_items row, so it would repeat once per row and a sum over the mart would count it several times (order amount and line amount are different levels).
-- Left out: customers.name: looks like personal data (P1); add it here if the mart may show it.
-- TODO (customer): what counts as revenue or an order amount. order_items.quantity is a quantity and order_items has no amount; products.list_price is a price in reach. The price comes from products.list_price, one row per products, as it stands at query time: a list price, not necessarily the price paid, and a later change of it changes the history. Check against an invoiced amount if there is one. No amount is computed here.
-- TODO (customer): the business rules are not in the metadata (what counts as revenue, which statuses, cancelled or returned rows, currency); add them as filters and columns here.

{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select
    f.[order_id] as [order_id],
    f.[line_no] as [line_no],
    f.[product_id] as [product_id],
    f.[quantity] as [quantity],
    d1.[order_id] as [orders_order_id],
    d1.[customer_id] as [orders_customer_id],
    d1.[order_date] as [orders_order_date],
    d1.[ship_to_id] as [orders_ship_to_id],
    d2.[product_id] as [products_product_id],
    d2.[name] as [products_name],
    d2.[category_id] as [products_category_id],
    d3.[id] as [categories_id],
    d3.[name] as [categories_name],
    d4.[customer_id] as [customers_customer_id],
    d4.[country] as [customers_country]
from {{ ref('stg_shop__order_items') }} as f
left join {{ ref('stg_shop__orders') }} as d1
    on f.[order_id] = d1.[order_id]
left join {{ ref('stg_shop__products') }} as d2
    on f.[product_id] = d2.[product_id]
left join {{ ref('stg_shop__categories') }} as d3
    on d2.[category_id] = d3.[id]
left join {{ ref('stg_shop__customers') }} as d4
    on d1.[customer_id] = d4.[customer_id]
nodes.label: fct_order_items

nodes.code:
-- fct_orders: one row per orders row (order_id).
-- Generated by Krusgraph for dbt-fabric 1.12 (Fabric Data Warehouse T-SQL). A draft: review it. Nothing was created or run.
-- Joined only over relationships whose target key was counted unique (many-to-one), each over its safest path:
--   orders.customer_id -> customers.customer_id (R1): holds for all 60 rows with a value
-- Left out: customers.name: looks like personal data (P1); add it here if the mart may show it.
-- TODO (customer): the business rules are not in the metadata (what counts as revenue, which statuses, cancelled or returned rows, currency); add them as filters and columns here.

{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select
    f.[order_id] as [order_id],
    f.[customer_id] as [customer_id],
    f.[order_date] as [order_date],
    f.[ship_to_id] as [ship_to_id],
    d1.[customer_id] as [customers_customer_id],
    d1.[country] as [customers_country],
    a1.[order_items_rows] as [order_items_rows],
    a1.[order_items_quantity_sum] as [order_items_quantity_sum]
from {{ ref('stg_shop__orders') }} as f
left join {{ ref('stg_shop__customers') }} as d1
    on f.[customer_id] = d1.[customer_id]
left join (
    -- order_items summed to one row per orders before the join (order_items.order_id -> orders.order_id (R1)), so no orders row repeats
    select [order_id], count(*) as [order_items_rows], sum([quantity]) as [order_items_quantity_sum]
    from {{ ref('stg_shop__order_items') }}
    group by [order_id]
) as a1
    on f.[order_id] = a1.[order_id]
nodes.label: fct_orders

findings.proposed_fix: None in silver: products.list_price already sits on products, one row per products row. Sum it once per products row (the query summed_per_header), never over the joined order_items rows. Which level the amount belongs to is the business decision below.

questions.ask: Is products.list_price a value of each products row (sum it once per products row), or does it belong to each order_items row?
options: of products: reports sum it on products (summed_per_header)
of each order_items row: it belongs in order_items, and the source owner says how it splits
not summed at all (a price or a rate)

findings.what_is_wrong: products.list_price sits on products, and order_items has up to 27 row(s) per products row: a report that joins the two and sums list_price counts it once per order_items row (a fan-out).

findings.proposed_fix: None: Without a key there is nothing to de-duplicate on; the silver draft copies the rows as they are.

findings.do_instead: Aggregate list_price on products (one row per products) and join the result, or sum a order_items amount; never SUM(products.list_price) over order_items rows.
findings.explanation: products.list_price is an amount on products, and order_items has 16.75 rows for each row of products on average and up to 27 (8 referenced header value(s), 8 of them in products) (rule R1: order_items.product_id → products.product_id). In a join of the two, each products amount is repeated on every order_items row, so SUM(products.list_price) over the joined rows counts each products row once per order_items row and comes out too large; by how much depends on the amounts, because the products rows have between 13 and 27 order_items rows each, and the average number of rows is not the ratio of the two sums. Sum it on products itself, or sum an amount of order_items instead: order amount and line amount are different levels.

amount_levels.note: Names and types say where an amount sits; whether a report sums it over the lines is not in the plan. The counts are over the whole tables at the moment of the call.
amount_levels.rule: A number on the header table of a many-to-one relationship is repeated on every line row in a join of the two; summing it over the joined rows counts each header once per line.

plan.name: shop

rules.K2: a column named `id`, `no`, `nr`, `<table>_id`, `<table>id`, `<singular>_id`, `<singular>id`, `<table>_key`, `<table>_code`, `<table>_nr`, `<table>_no`, `<table>_sk`, `<table>_bk`, or an abbreviation of the table name (four letters or more) with one of those suffixes (`<table>snr` too: the Swedish genitive, `Leverantorsnr` in `Leverantor`); a leading `dim_`/`fact_`/`tbl_` is not part of the table's name; when nothing matches literally, the same through the synonym table (`KundNr` in `kunder`, `cust_id` in `dim_customer`), reported under `synonyms`
rules.K3: nothing — the table gets no key; it can be queried but not by pk, and nothing can point at it
rules.K4: junction: no column names a key and the table starts with two or more reference columns; together they are the key (not applied to history tables with a start_*/valid_from/effective_* column)
rules.K5: line: no column names a key; the reference to the header table plus a line-number column (line_no, position, seq…)
rules.R1: column named `<B>_id` / `<B>id` / `<singular B>_id` / `<singular B>id` (also _key, _code, _nr, _no, _sk, _bk) where B has a single key
rules.R2: column has exactly the same name as B's single key column, and that name is not just `id`
rules.R3: all of B's composite key columns appear in A
rules.R4: weaker name match when R1 and R2 find nothing: the R1/R2 shapes through the synonym table (`Kunde_ID` → `Kunden`, `cust_id` → `customers`, noted on the relationship), a role before B's name (`manager_staff_id` → staff), or an abbreviation of B of four letters or more (`o_custkey` → customer); never across suffixes (`wwi_order_id` does not point at a table keyed by `order_key`)
rules.R5: checked against the rows: a code column `<stem>_code` / `<stem>_no` / `<stem>_key` where a table with the same stem (singular/plural, snake/camel) has the key `code`/`no`/`key`, or a role name (`ship_to_id`, `created_by`, `approved_by`) whose role word says what the table holds; planned only when every value is in that table's key, the type family is the same, there are two or more distinct values and one table qualifies, otherwise proposed with the reason
rules.confirmed: given by the caller in `confirmed=[...]`, applied as-is, before inference

7 tables, 6 with keys, 6 relationships
no key (query only; can reference others, cannot be referenced): audit_log

questions.sql:
SELECT t.[name] AS [name], COUNT(*) AS [rows]
FROM [shop].[orders] AS s
JOIN [shop].[customers] AS t ON s.[customer_id] = t.[customer_id]
GROUP BY t.[name]
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC
LIMIT 10
questions.title: How many orders rows per customers?
questions.why: orders.customer_id points at customers (rule R1); name names each customers row.

questions.sql:
SELECT t.[name] AS [name], SUM(s.[quantity]) AS [total_quantity]
FROM [shop].[order_items] AS s
JOIN [shop].[products] AS t ON s.[product_id] = t.[product_id]
GROUP BY t.[name]
ORDER BY SUM(s.[quantity]) DESC
LIMIT 10
questions.title: Total quantity per products
questions.why: quantity is a number in order_items that is neither its key nor a reference; summed over the R1 link to products.

questions.sql:
SELECT t.[name] AS [name]
FROM [shop].[customers] AS t
LEFT JOIN [shop].[orders] AS s ON s.[customer_id] = t.[customer_id]
WHERE s.[customer_id] IS NULL
ORDER BY t.[name]
LIMIT 10
questions.title: Which customers have no orders?
questions.why: Rows of customers that nothing in orders points at: often the first data-quality question a customer asks.

questions.sql:
SELECT substr([order_date], 1, 7) AS [month], COUNT(*) AS [rows]
FROM [shop].[orders]
WHERE [order_date] IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY substr([order_date], 1, 7)
ORDER BY substr([order_date], 1, 7) DESC
LIMIT 12
questions.title: Rows in orders per month
questions.why: order_date is a date column; the month profile shows how far the data reaches and where the gaps are.

questions.sql:
SELECT t0.[address_id] AS [addresses_address_id], t5.[id], t5.[name]
FROM [shop].[addresses] AS t0
JOIN [shop].[customers] AS t1 ON t0.[customer_id] = t1.[customer_id]
JOIN [shop].[orders] AS t2 ON t1.[customer_id] = t2.[customer_id]
JOIN [shop].[order_items] AS t3 ON t2.[order_id] = t3.[order_id]
JOIN [shop].[products] AS t4 ON t3.[product_id] = t4.[product_id]
JOIN [shop].[categories] AS t5 ON t4.[category_id] = t5.[id]
LIMIT 10
questions.title: From addresses to categories in one query
questions.why: The longest shortest path in the graph: addresses → customers → orders → order_items → products → categories. join_path writes this SQL.
